mcqs.question: A candidate has never managed anyone and worries they have no leadership stories. What's the right reframe?
options: They should decline this question and redirect to a different category
They should describe a time they were assigned a hard technical task and completed it well
They should look for moments where their own call, not a formal role, is what moved an outcome others acted on
Leadership questions only apply to candidates who have held a management title
mcqs.explanation: Leadership is scored as a behavior — driving outcomes through others — not a role with a reporting line, so an IC with zero reports can have strong leadership stories. Completing an assigned task well, without anyone else's behavior changing, doesn't demonstrate this on its own.

mcqs.question: Which statement demonstrates a real influence tactic rather than bare assertion?
options: "Getting a respected engineer on their team to co-review the proposal is what got the lead to take the meeting."
"I explained clearly why my proposal was the right one."
"I was persistent and eventually they came around."
"I was confident in my technical judgment, so they trusted me."
mcqs.explanation: Naming the specific mechanism — an ally's credibility opening a door — is a checkable tactic (alliance-building). The other options assert persuasion happened without naming what actually caused the shift, which reads as filler rather than a demonstrated skill.

mcqs.question: In the skeptical-stakeholder worked example, why did letting the team lead present the pilot findings to his own engineers work better than the platform team announcing the migration directly?
options: It avoided the platform team doing any of the migration work
It let the message come from someone his team already trusted, converting a blocker into a distributor of the recommendation
It skipped the need to address his actual objection about migration cost
It made the decision look mandated rather than optional
mcqs.explanation: Letting the skeptic bring the finding to his own team leveraged existing trust and turned an initial blocker into an advocate — the underlying cost objection was still addressed first via the pilot data, and the point was specifically to avoid it looking like a top-down mandate.

mcqs.question: A candidate answers "tell me about a time you influenced without authority" by describing getting their own direct reports to adopt a new process. Why does this likely miss the mark?
options: Because direct reports never actually follow a manager's direction
Because the question specifically tests generating followership without a reporting line backing you, which this story doesn't demonstrate
Because the story should instead be about a peer manager, not direct reports
Because processes, unlike technical decisions, don't count as valid leadership topics
mcqs.explanation: The prompt isolates whether you can move people absent formal authority; a manager directing their own reports has that authority available, so the story doesn't test the intended skill — regardless of whether the process itself was a good one or who else it could have involved.

mcqs.question: A candidate describes building an internal tool entirely alone, with no one else's workflow changing as a result, and calls it their leadership story. What's the issue?
options: Solo-built tools can never be technically impressive enough to use in an interview
It should have taken less time to build to count
Leadership requires someone else's behavior changing because of you; self-directed work alone doesn't establish that
It's a fine leadership story as long as the tool is still in use today
mcqs.explanation: Self-direction is valuable but distinct from leadership, which requires demonstrating followership — someone else moved because of you. A story where removing every other person changes nothing about the outcome belongs under ownership or technical depth, not leadership, regardless of how long it took or whether it's still used.

mcqs.question: What distinguishes a senior/staff-caliber leadership story from a junior-scoped one, according to this topic?
options: The senior story involves a larger number of people in the initial rollout
The senior story shows the outcome persisting or spreading after the candidate stopped actively driving it
The senior story avoids naming any specific tactic used to gain agreement
The senior story is measured by how quickly the initial adoption happened
mcqs.explanation: The strongest signal is durability and spread beyond your continued involvement — a practice still running or adopted elsewhere without your ongoing push. Headcount at rollout, omitting tactics, or adoption speed don't capture this; a large team adopting something that dies the moment you leave is not the senior signal.
